title: Azure Virtual Desktop Hybrid Reaches GA with Licensing Details Unpublished
gist: Microsoft made Azure Virtual Desktop Hybrid generally available, letting customers run session hosts on their own on-prem hardware via Azure Arc while Azure handles brokering, but shipped without publishing the separate AVD Hybrid service-license pricing, and a partner testing since Ignite 2025 says a Software Assurance requirement on RDS CALs alone disqualifies roughly 90% of prospective customer deployments.

insights.claim: Azure Virtual Desktop Hybrid runs session hosts on the customer's own hardware and hypervisor, connected through Azure Arc, while session brokering and management stay in Azure; pricing follows that split with per-user licensing for the service and compute/storage/networking costs remaining on-premises.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: A hybrid VDI model that lets enterprises keep capex on-prem while paying Microsoft only for the control-plane/brokering layer — relevant to comparing TCO against fully cloud-hosted AVD or Windows 365.
insights.locator: Session hosts run on the customer's own hardware

insights.claim: The capability progressed from limited preview (extending beyond Azure Local to Hyper-V, Nutanix AHV, VMware vSphere, and physical Windows Servers) to public preview in March 2026 to GA, with the architecture unchanged: all communication is outbound over HTTPS, removing the need for inbound connectivity.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Outbound-only HTTPS architecture simplifies firewall/security posture for regulated on-prem environments deploying this hybrid model.
insights.locator: InfoQ covered the limited preview in November

insights.claim: What changed at GA is that the deployment path is now documented rather than gated behind an interest form — creating a VM, installing/configuring Azure Arc, installing the extension, and selecting a host pool can all be done from the Azure portal.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Self-service GA rollout removes friction for adoption, but the pricing gap (below) may blunt near-term uptake despite easier provisioning.
insights.locator: What has changed is that the deployment path

themes.theme: Pricing and licensing gap at launch

insights.claim: Azure Virtual Desktop Hybrid requires OS user entitlement licensing plus a separate Azure Virtual Desktop Hybrid service license, and Microsoft's documentation says pricing details on the second license are still to come, with four of the first announcement commenters immediately asking about it.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Microsoft shipped a GA product without publishing its own pricing — a notable go-to-market misstep that stalls enterprise budget planning and procurement decisions immediately post-launch.
insights.quote: As others already said, pricing is going to be the key here.
insights.locator: Azure Virtual Desktop Hybrid requires OS user

insights.claim: A partner testing Hybrid since Ignite 2025 says the documentation supports Windows Server only when RDS Client Access Licenses carry Software Assurance, a requirement that alone reportedly disqualifies around 90% of their potential customer deployments because most customers lack SA on their RDS CALs or recently bought CALs for Windows Server 2025/2022 without SA, making relicensing to RDS User Subscription uneconomical.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: A specific, quantified licensing gate (90% disqualification) is a material near-term revenue ceiling on this product line unless Microsoft relaxes the SA-on-RDS-CAL requirement.
insights.quote: This requirement alone kills around 90% of our potential customer deployments since most of our customers have no SA on their RDS CALs or have recently purchased RDS CALs with Windows Server 2025 / 2022 without SA, so a relicensing to RDS User Subscription is not economically feasable.
insights.locator: A partner who has been testing Hybrid

insights.claim: The same partner questioned whether the required Hybrid user license fee is charged on top of RDS CALs (double charge) or could instead absorb the Software Assurance requirement, and Windows 11/Windows 10 Enterprise multi-session are not supported on Hybrid, meaning the licensing model underpinning most existing Azure Virtual Desktop deployments does not carry over.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Lack of multi-session support compounds the licensing gate and materially changes the compute-density economics versus standard cloud-hosted AVD.
insights.locator: That constraint compounds a second one

insights.claim: Because multi-session Windows 11/10 isn't supported on Hybrid, density suffers: Microsoft's own cloud AVD examples show two users per vCPU for Office workloads and six per vCPU for call-center/data-entry work versus a full VM per user (2 vCPUs, 4GB) for single-session, meaning a thousand knowledge workers need several times the compute on Hybrid, absorbed by hardware the customer already owns or must buy.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Quantifies the hidden hardware cost multiplier (several times more compute) that on-prem customers must budget for beyond the advertised per-user service license.

insights.claim: Preview feedback repeatedly requested Windows 11 multi-session support, with one viewer noting the direct commercial consequence of adding it: they could onboard more customers.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Strong, repeated customer/partner demand signal for a specific missing feature (multi-session) that Microsoft could add to unlock adoption.
insights.quote: Good move. I could onboard more customers with this. Even more if you added win11 multi.
insights.locator: Preview feedback said the same thing repeatedly

insights.claim: Azure Virtual Desktop Hybrid does not provision or manage virtual machine state, ruling out power management, autoscale, Start VM on Connect, and Session Host Configuration; organizations must manage their own session hosts using hypervisor tools, scripts, or partner solutions — explaining why partners like Nerdio and Login VSI are filling the operational layer Azure natively supplies for cloud-hosted session hosts.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Creates a direct revenue opportunity for third-party VDI management vendors (Nerdio, Login VSI) to fill the operational gap Azure leaves open in the hybrid model.
insights.locator: A third set of gaps sits in what the service

insights.claim: Nerdio's chief product and technology officer described Hybrid as a more flexible path toward Windows 365, naming compliance requirements, cost constraints, and sunk infrastructure spend as the reasons organizations are not yet ready for a full cloud migration.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Positions AVD Hybrid as a transitional/bridge product feeding eventual migration to Windows 365 rather than a permanent architecture, useful for forecasting Microsoft's longer-term VDI roadmap.
insights.locator: Scott Manchester, chief product and technology officer

insights.claim: Session hosts need outbound access to login.microsoftonline.com for authentication and to *.wvd.microsoft.com for service traffic and RDP connectivity, and Microsoft states that blocking these required endpoints is unsupported, meaning the on-prem desktops remain dependent on Azure even though they run locally.
insights.speaker: Steef-Jan Wiggers
insights.so_what: Even 'on-prem' AVD Hybrid deployments retain a hard cloud dependency for auth/brokering, meaning air-gapped or fully sovereign deployments are not possible with this architecture — relevant for regulated/data-residency buyers evaluating the regulated-workload use case.
insights.locator: The dependency that is created is documented
